scenes.narration: Subnets have appeared in every network lab so far — inline inside the VNet in lab six, generated by for each in the last two. This lesson slows down and writes them by hand, one resource per tier, and shows why the standalone form is the one real networks are built with.

Here's what you'll learn. One: azurerm subnet as its own resource — one per tier. Two: standalone subnets versus the inline subnets block of lab six. Three: why separate resources unlock network security groups, delegations, and service endpoints. Four: an output that hands the subnet I D to later labs.

This is lab twelve. Lab six tucked subnets inside the VNet block. The last two labs generated them from a map. Both work — but both assume subnets are interchangeable. When each tier needs different treatment, its own firewall, its own delegation, you write them out, one resource each. That's today's form.

Why does the standalone form matter? Because a subnet that is its own resource has an identity — an I D that other resources can reference. An inline subnet belongs to the VNet; there's nothing to point a security group at. The moment a subnet needs to be treated as a thing — firewalled, delegated, peered — it has to stand alone. That's the form this lesson builds, and the form the coming N I C and N S G labs rely on.

As always, the lab is in the course GitHub repository under Section 1, Foundations, with the link in the description. This one is deliberately small — readme, main dot t f, terraform dot t f — because the lesson is about form, not volume.

The setup first, and one absence matters. Locals name the region and the group. The VNet is created with its ten eighty slash sixteen space — but look at what's missing. There is no subnets block inside it. The VNet holds the address space and stops there.

Then the subnets, and each one is a full, standalone resource. The web subnet — group name, VNet name, its own prefix. And the app subnet, the same pattern for the second tier. This is lab six's network, rebuilt in the explicit form. Two blocks instead of one, but every subnet is now independently addressable.

One output closes the file: the web subnet's I D. Hold onto it — it's the handle the next lab's network interface will attach to. A resource with an I D is a resource that can be connected to other resources.

Drawn out: the VNet carries the address space and no subnets. Each subnet is its own resource referencing the VNet, and the web subnet's I D flows out as the handle for later labs. The explicit form buys addressability.

Apply time, and the plan reads like the diagram: group, VNet, then two subnets, each its own line, each its own resource. The output hands back the web subnet's full Azure resource path. That I D is the entire point of the standalone form — the next lab consumes it.

The pitfall: going back to inline subnets for anything beyond a quick demo. The inline block is compact, but it welds the subnet to the VNet — and the day you need a per-subnet firewall, there's no standalone resource to attach it to. So choose by shape: many identical tiers, for each with a map. A few distinct tiers that grow in different directions, write them out. When in doubt, standalone is the safer default.

Quick recap. Today we wrote subnets the standalone way: one resource per tier, the VNet carrying only the address space. Each subnet gained an identity — an I D other resources can reference — and we exported the web subnet's as the handle for what comes next: a network interface.
Now that we understand how this Terraform configuration works, in the next part of this video, we'll move to a real-world demo and deploy it in Microsoft Azure.
